OVERVIEW

[1] I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Honduras.
a. The Appellant claims refugee protection in Canada because he fears persecution in Honduras on the basis of his sexual orientation and that he would be killed by the maras (criminal gangs) because he has refused to joint them.
b. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that there is insufficient credible evidence to establish that the claimant is gay or bisexual, or that he was perceived as such in Honduras.1
c. The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant is not credible.
d. The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in Finding that the Appellant is not credible.
e. I find that the RPD did not err. I find that there is insufficient credible evidence to support a conclusion that the Appellant is homosexual or bisexual as he claims to be or that he would be harmed by criminal gangs.
DECISION

[2] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention2 refugee nor a person in need of protection.

On January 4, 2019, the RAD overturned the first RPD decision, substituting a determination that the Appellant is not excluded under Article 1F(b) and returning the case to the RPD to assess whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

[11] A second RPD Panel found that the Appellant is not a Convention Refugee nor a person in need of protection in a decision dated December 30, 2019. The Appellant has appealed this RPD decision.
INTERVENTION BY MINISTER

[12] The Minister intervened in writing at the RAD. The Minister's arguments are summarized as follows:
1. The Minister submits that the findings on law and fact in the RPD decision support the RAD Panel confirming that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee, and that he is not a person in need of protection.
2. Pursuant to RAD Rule 4(3)(c)(ii) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules6 (RAD Rules), the decision the Minister wants the RAD to make is to dismiss the Appellant's appeal, and to confirm the RPD decision pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act7 (IRPA). Hence, the Minister disagrees with the order sought by the Appellant at paragraph 23 of his Memorandum.
3. It was open to the RPD Panel, based on its credibility findings, to find the Appellant's claim to be clearly fraudulent; and therefore, this is a manifestly unfounded claim pursuant to section 107.1 of the IRPA.8 This option is also available to the RAD when confirming the RPD's decision, and the Minister supports that finding.9

[13] The Appellant has responded to the Minister's submission. I will consider both the Minister's submission and the Appellants response in the analysis that follows.
Manifestly unfounded claim

[14] The Minister submits that it was open to the RPD to find that the Appellant's claim is manifestly unfounded. The Minister further submits that it is open to the RAD to find that the present claim is manifestly unfounded, and the Minister supports the RAD making such a finding. The Appellant argues that the facts of the case do not support finding that the claim is manifestly unfounded.

[15] I do not agree with the Minister. I find that the RAD does not have the jurisdiction to find that the Appellant's claim is manifestly unfounded. In reaching this finding, I have relied upon my own analysis and RAD jurisprudence in a similar case.10

[16] Section 107.1 of the IRPA provides as follows:
If the Refugee Protection Division rejects a claim for refugee protection, it must state in its reasons for the decision that the claim is manifestly unfounded if it is of the opinion that the claim is clearly fraudulent [RAD emphasis added].

[17] As is underscored in the above, the authority to state that a claim for refugee protection is manifestly unfounded is conferred by the IRPA upon the RPD. As there are no other provisions in the IRPA that specifically confer a similar authority on the RAD, I find that the RAD does not have the statutory authority to state that the Appellant's claim is manifestly unfounded.

The RPD found that the presumption of truthfulness had been rebutted with respect to the Appellant. I agree with the RPD. I consider the problems with the Appellant's testimony in the analysis that follow.
The Appellant's sexual orientation

[24] In Ward,16 the Supreme Court of Canada recognized that sexual orientation can be characterized as a particular social group. This extends to gender identity and expression.17

[25] The Appellant argues that he faces persecution in Honduras because he is gay as he claimed in his initial BOC, or because he is bisexual as he claimed in his amended BOC and in his testimony. The Appellant's sexual orientation is central to his claim.

[26] The RPD found that there is insufficient credible evidence to establish that the Appellant is gay or bisexual, or that he would be perceived as such.18

[27] The Appellant argues on appeal that: "He is a bisexual man, and if this fact is discovered in Honduras, his life will be at risk from the Maras, and he will be discriminated to the point of persecution by society at large."19

[28] The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant was not credible because the Appellant's testimony about his sexual orientation contained inconsistencies, omissions and lacked coherence. The Appellants argue on appeal that RPD erred because:
If anything, the Applicant's testimony is consistent with what is stated in the SOGIE Guidelines, in that a person's understanding of their sexual orientation may change. That is precisely what is reflected in the Applicant's testimony. Rather than being inconsistent, he was simply explaining how his sexual orientation has evolved since he first realized he was bisexual as a young teenager.20

[29] The Chairperson's Guideline on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE Guideline) defines sexual orientation as: "A person's physical, romantic and/or emotional attraction to, and/or intimate relations with, individuals of a different gender, the same gender, no gender, or more than one gender. A person's understanding of their sexual orientation may change [RAD Emphasis]."21

[30] At paragraphs 26-31, the RPD drew a negative inference about the Appellant's credibility because he initially indicated in his testimony that he prefers men and felt this way since he was 13 or 14 years old, but after several follow-questions he stated that he is not attracted to men and only indicated that he is bisexual because he used to feel that way when he was 13 or 14. The RPD found that there was no reasonable explanation for these inconsistencies. In relation to this finding, the Appellant argues that there is nothing inconsistent in terms of the Appellant's account of his sexual orientation (paragraphs 10-14 of Appellant's Record).

[31] The Appellant argues that his understanding of his sexual orientation changed over time. On appeal, the Appellant cites the following exchange with the RPD Panel:
RPD: What do you feel and want now?
Appellant: The attraction for men has gone [RAD Emphasis]. Since I came here to Canada, I have never had any relationship, any interaction with men. And now I also dedicate myself more to my family, to my future wife. And I wouldn't like my relationship to be broken for that kind of situation.22

[32] The Appellant argues on appeal that he is still attracted to men because he has testified that he watches same-sex male pornography. The Appellant argues this is not inconsistent with his testimony that he does not have any ongoing attraction to men because he wants to dedicate himself to his future wife.

[33] The Appellant testified that he had one intimate relationship during the almost three years he was in the US. He testified that he was in a relationship with a woman that lasted for one year and that this was his sole intimate relationship in the US.23 The Appellant testified that he had a one-time same-sex experience with a man in the US. The Appellant testified that he did not like it and that he "wouldn't like that to happen again."24 The Appellant testified that the encounter was consensual "And it was not like I wanted to do it. It was like something more like -- it was the curiosity or something."25

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Honduras.
a. The Appellant claims refugee protection in Canada because he fears persecution in Honduras on the basis of his sexual orientation and that he would be killed by the maras (criminal gangs) because he has refused to joint them.
b. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that there is insufficient credible evidence to establish that the claimant is gay or bisexual, or that he was perceived as such in Honduras.1
c. The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant is not credible.
d. The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in Finding that the Appellant is not credible.
e. I find that the RPD did not err. I find that there is insufficient credible evidence to support a conclusion that the Appellant is homosexual or bisexual as he claims to be or that he would be harmed by criminal gangs.
DECISION
[2] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention2 refugee nor a person in need of protection.
BACKGROUND
[3] The Appellant was born in Honduras on XXXX XXXX, 1995.

[4] The Appellant left Honduras in XXXX 2012 and entered the United States (US) in XXXX 2012 where he was detained by US immigration authorities. Upon his release from immigration detention, the Appellant lived in the US until XXXX 2015.

[5] According to documents submitted with his Basis of Claim (BOC), the Appellant crossed into Canada from the US in XXXX 2015 at a place other than an official port of entry.3 The Appellant did not make a claim for refugee protection in Canada upon arrival.
CASE HISTORY

[6] The RPD Panel summarized the facts of the case from paragraph 2 to paragraph 11of the RPD decision.4 The Appellant cites this summary in his Memorandum without objection.5 I agree with the RPD Panel's background summary. I summarize it as follow.

[7] According to documents received from the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness (The Minister), the Appellant came to their attention on November 6, 2016 after being arrested by New Westminster Police following an altercation outside a bar.
[8] The Appellant's BOC form was received by the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) on November 23, 2016.

[9] The Minister intervened in the claim. The claim was initially heard by the RPD on January 18, 2017. On January 27, 2017, the first RPD Panel refused the claim, excluding the Appellant from refugee protection pursuant to Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention. This first RPD Panel found that that there were serious reasons for considering that the Appellant committed a serious non-political crime in the US. This first RPD decision was upheld by the RAD on February 28, 2018.

[10] The Federal Court granted the judicial review and the case was returned to the RAD for redetermination by a different member. On January 4, 2019, the RAD overturned the first RPD decision, substituting a determination that the Appellant is not excluded under Article 1F(b) and returning the case to the RPD to assess whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

[11] A second RPD Panel found that the Appellant is not a Convention Refugee nor a person in need of protection in a decision dated December 30, 2019. The Appellant has appealed this RPD decision.
INTERVENTION BY MINISTER

[12] The Minister intervened in writing at the RAD. The Minister's arguments are summarized as follows:
1. The Minister submits that the findings on law and fact in the RPD decision support the RAD Panel confirming that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee, and that he is not a person in need of protection.
2. Pursuant to RAD Rule 4(3)(c)(ii) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules6 (RAD Rules), the decision the Minister wants the RAD to make is to dismiss the Appellant's appeal, and to confirm the RPD decision pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act7 (IRPA). Hence, the Minister disagrees with the order sought by the Appellant at paragraph 23 of his Memorandum.
3. It was open to the RPD Panel, based on its credibility findings, to find the Appellant's claim to be clearly fraudulent; and therefore, this is a manifestly unfounded claim pursuant to section 107.1 of the IRPA.8 This option is also available to the RAD when confirming the RPD's decision, and the Minister supports that finding.9

[13] The Appellant has responded to the Minister's submission. I will consider both the Minister's submission and the Appellants response in the analysis that follows.
Manifestly unfounded claim

[14] The Minister submits that it was open to the RPD to find that the Appellant's claim is manifestly unfounded. The Minister further submits that it is open to the RAD to find that the present claim is manifestly unfounded, and the Minister supports the RAD making such a finding. The Appellant argues that the facts of the case do not support finding that the claim is manifestly unfounded.

[15] I do not agree with the Minister. I find that the RAD does not have the jurisdiction to find that the Appellant's claim is manifestly unfounded. In reaching this finding, I have relied upon my own analysis and RAD jurisprudence in a similar case.10

[16] Section 107.1 of the IRPA provides as follows:
If the Refugee Protection Division rejects a claim for refugee protection, it must state in its reasons for the decision that the claim is manifestly unfounded if it is of the opinion that the claim is clearly fraudulent [RAD emphasis added].

[17] As is underscored in the above, the authority to state that a claim for refugee protection is manifestly unfounded is conferred by the IRPA upon the RPD. As there are no other provisions in the IRPA that specifically confer a similar authority on the RAD, I find that the RAD does not have the statutory authority to state that the Appellant's claim is manifestly unfounded.
Oral hearing

[18] The Appellants have requested an oral hearing pursuant to section 110(6) of the IRPA11 if any documentary evidence is submitted at the RAD. Section 110(6) of the IRPA provides that the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred in section 110(3)12 that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal; that is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim; and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. This subsection is discretionary given the term "may". This subsection is also conjunctive: all three elements must be present before a hearing may be held.

[19] In this case, no new evidence that meets the requirements of section 110(3) has been submitted. Therefore, because all three elements of the test for an oral hearing are not met, there is no jurisdiction for the RAD to hold an oral hearing. The RAD denies the request for an oral hearing.
ANALYSIS
[20] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.13 As part of my analysis, I have conducted an independent assessment of the evidence and the arguments.14

[21] When a person swears to the truth of certain allegations before the IRB, there is a presumption that those allegations are true unless there is a reason to doubt their truthfulness. This presumption of truthfulness does not apply to inferences or conclusions a witness may draw from facts, or to speculation for which there is no evidentiary basis.15

[22] The presumption that a person's sworn testimony is true may be rebutted where problems are identified with the testimony. These problems can include contradictions, inconsistencies, and omissions; incoherent or vague testimony; limited knowledge of key elements of the case; or a reliance on false documents.
Appellant's credibility

[23] The RPD found that there are numerous credibility problems with the Appellant's testimony before the RPD. The RPD found that the presumption of truthfulness had been rebutted with respect to the Appellant. I agree with the RPD. I consider the problems with the Appellant's testimony in the analysis that follow.
The Appellant's sexual orientation
[24] In Ward,16 the Supreme Court of Canada recognized that sexual orientation can be characterized as a particular social group. This extends to gender identity and expression.17

[25] The Appellant argues that he faces persecution in Honduras because he is gay as he claimed in his initial BOC, or because he is bisexual as he claimed in his amended BOC and in his testimony. The Appellant's sexual orientation is central to his claim.
[26] The RPD found that there is insufficient credible evidence to establish that the Appellant is gay or bisexual, or that he would be perceived as such.18

[27] The Appellant argues on appeal that: "He is a bisexual man, and if this fact is discovered in Honduras, his life will be at risk from the Maras, and he will be discriminated to the point of persecution by society at large."19

[28] The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant was not credible because the Appellant's testimony about his sexual orientation contained inconsistencies, omissions and lacked coherence. The Appellants argue on appeal that RPD erred because:
If anything, the Applicant's testimony is consistent with what is stated in the SOGIE Guidelines, in that a person's understanding of their sexual orientation may change. That is precisely what is reflected in the Applicant's testimony. Rather than being inconsistent, he was simply explaining how his sexual orientation has evolved since he first realized he was bisexual as a young teenager.20

[29] The Chairperson's Guideline on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE Guideline) defines sexual orientation as: "A person's physical, romantic and/or emotional attraction to, and/or intimate relations with, individuals of a different gender, the same gender, no gender, or more than one gender. A person's understanding of their sexual orientation may change [RAD Emphasis]."21

[30] At paragraphs 26-31, the RPD drew a negative inference about the Appellant's credibility because he initially indicated in his testimony that he prefers men and felt this way since he was 13 or 14 years old, but after several follow-questions he stated that he is not attracted to men and only indicated that he is bisexual because he used to feel that way when he was 13 or 14. The RPD found that there was no reasonable explanation for these inconsistencies. In relation to this finding, the Appellant argues that there is nothing inconsistent in terms of the Appellant's account of his sexual orientation (paragraphs 10-14 of Appellant's Record).

[31] The Appellant argues that his understanding of his sexual orientation changed over time. On appeal, the Appellant cites the following exchange with the RPD Panel:
RPD: What do you feel and want now?
Appellant: The attraction for men has gone [RAD Emphasis]. Since I came here to Canada, I have never had any relationship, any interaction with men. And now I also dedicate myself more to my family, to my future wife. And I wouldn't like my relationship to be broken for that kind of situation.22

[32] The Appellant argues on appeal that he is still attracted to men because he has testified that he watches same-sex male pornography. The Appellant argues this is not inconsistent with his testimony that he does not have any ongoing attraction to men because he wants to dedicate himself to his future wife.

[33] The Appellant testified that he had one intimate relationship during the almost three years he was in the US. He testified that he was in a relationship with a woman that lasted for one year and that this was his sole intimate relationship in the US.23 The Appellant testified that he had a one-time same-sex experience with a man in the US. The Appellant testified that he did not like it and that he "wouldn't like that to happen again."24 The Appellant testified that the encounter was consensual "And it was not like I wanted to do it. It was like something more like -- it was the curiosity or something."25

[34] I do not agree with the Appellant's argument that the RPD erred in its credibility assessment. The issue is not that the Appellant's understanding of his sexual orientation evolved over the course of his lifetime, but rather that the Appellant's testimony regarding his sexual orientation evolved during the RPD hearing and that his testimony contains significant inconsistencies. For the reasons that follow, I find that the RPD did not err.

[35] I have conducted my own analysis of the Appellant's testimony at the RPD. I agree with the RPD Panel that there are significant issues with the Appellant's testimony that undermine his credibility.

[36] Even were I to accept the Appellant's testimony as truthful, I am not persuaded that he is bisexual as he claims to be. The Appellant testified that he is bisexual because he had adolescent fantasies about men when he was 14 or 15. He testified that he liked men's physical appearance and dress. When the RPD asked him why he considered himself bisexual, the Appellant testified he considered himself bisexual because he used to be attracted to men. The Appellant testified that he had a single consensual sexual encounter in the US but that the encounter was not enjoyable, and he had no wish to repeat it.

[37] The Appellant has testified that he does not wish to have sexual relations with men nor is he attracted sexually to men. The Appellant grounds his claim to being bisexual on adolescent fantasies that were unfulfilled, on a single sexual episode with a man which he did not enjoy and does not wish to repeat, and on the fact that he like to watch pornography of men having sex. I find that the Appellants fondness for gay pornography does not establish that he has a sexual orientation that would subject him to harm in Honduras or that would require him to supress fundamental aspects of his personality in order to avoid harm.
SOGIE Terminology

[38] The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in making an adverse credibility finding because the Appellant used the terms "homosexual" and "bisexual" interchangeably in his BOC form, narrative, and during his interview with Canadian Border Services Agency (CBSA) officers in November 2016, despite providing testimony that he was aware of the differences between these terms at the time.26
[39] The RPD did not accept the Appellant's explanation that he was nervous and afraid of deportation when he was interviewed by CBSA officers and that this anxiety explains his word use.

[40] The RPD Panel cited a reference in the SOGIE Guideline that persons appearing before the RPD may not be familiar with SOGIE terminology. The RPD also noted that the Appellant testified that he knew the difference between the terms "homosexual" and "bisexual" before he left Honduras. The RPD drew "a further negative inference from the claimant's inconsistent and seemingly careless use of SOGIE terms about which he was knowledgeable."27

[41] I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in taking a negative inference. I accept the Appellant's explanation that he was under stress. I also note that English is not the Appellant's first language. I am also not persuaded that the Appellant was fully knowledgeable of the terms when he used them in his BOC form, his narrative and during his interview.

[42] I find that the Appellant's use of the words "homosexual" and "bisexual' in his BOC form, narrative and during his interaction with CBSA officers is not sufficient to support a negative credibility inference.

[43] Not withstanding this specific error on the part of the RPD, I agree with the RPD's overall credibility assessment. The Appellant's testimony regarding central elements of his claim contains significant inconsistencies and contradictions.
Letters from brother and mother

[44] The Appellant provided two letters from his mother and two letters from his brother to support his claim. The first version of each of the letters does not mention the Appellant's sexual orientation.

[45] The Appellant provided initial letters from his mother and his brother both dated XXXX XXXX, 2017 and XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016 respectively. The RPD notes that that these first letters do not refer to the Appellant's sexual orientation, The first letters refer to an alleged attempted gang recruitment of the Appellant by the maras and the intimidation and threats experienced by the Appellant's brother on the basis of his sexual orientation, however there is no mention of the Appellant's alleged bisexuality.

[46] The RPD found that "one would expect the claimant's mother and brother to mention the crucial detail of his sexual orientation in their initial letters of support."28 The Appellant testified at the RPD that he had told both his mother and his brother that he was bisexual before he came to Canada. The RPD considered the Appellant's explanation that his sexual orientation is a private matter, and his mother and brother did not want to offend him by including it in their initial letters. The RPD found this this explanation "incoherent and unreasonable"29 given that the letters were written to support the Appellant's claim for refugee protection. The RPD drew a negative inference from the Appellant's explanation.

[47] The Appellant provided the RPD with two subsequent letters, one each from his mother and his brother dated XXXX 2018. The second letters essentially repeat their allegations from the earlier letters with the addition of the Appellant's alleged sexual orientation. The Appellant testified at the RPD that his mother and brother provided the second letters dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, after they had become aware that the Appellant had claimed refugee protection in Canada on the basis of his sexual orientation.

[48] In her second letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, the Appellant's mother writes that once the Appellant left Honduras for the US, she took XXXX to Tegucigalpa because she didn't want "any one in my family and specially the gangs to know to know how my son [XXXX] felt."30 She writes that the Appellant, her son XXXX, told her he was bisexual XXXX months after he left Honduras when he was in the US.31 The Appellant testified at the RPD that the events in his mother's second letter occurred as described in her letter.

[49] The RPD found that the Appellant provided contradictory testimony about whether he discussed his sexual orientation with his mother, The Appellant initially testified at the RPD hearing that he never informed his mother about his sexual orientation, whereas the second letter from his mother indicates that the Appellant informed his mother that he is bisexual when he was in the US. The RPD put this to the Appellant but he "offered no explanation" why he had testified that he had never dared to tell his mother that he her was bisexual.32

[50] In his initial letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, the Appellant's brother XXXX says that gang members harassed him in front of the Appellant and his mother because of XXXX sexual orientation. XXXX does not mention in this letter that gang members harassed the Appellant. In response to questions from the RPD Panel regarding when XXXX told the Appellant he was gay, the Appellant testified that XXXX told the Appellant before the Appellant left Honduras for the US.

[51] In a second affidavit dated XXXX XXXX, 2018, the Appellant's brother, XXXX, writes that the Appellant told him he was bisexual in 2011 when the gangs tried to recruit the Appellant. The affidavit from XXXX dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016 relates very similar events to his 2018 affidavit but omits mention of the Appellant's sexual orientation.

[52] The RPD Panel asked the Appellant when he revealed to his gay brother that he was attracted to men himself. The Appellant replied that he told his brother that he was attracted to men once the Appellant was in the US.33 The RPD Panel put to the Appellant that this disclosure to his brother contradicted the Appellant's statement in Schedule A Form wherein he stated he had never talked to anyone about his sexual orientation. The Appellant explained that he completed the Schedule A Form in detention under pressure. I do not accept the Appellant's explanation for the contradiction. The Appellant's understanding of his sexual orientation and who he had told about it are central to his claim.

[53] I am unable to reconcile the contradictions between the affidavits and the Appellant's testimony regarding events that are core to the Appellant's claim that he is gay or bisexual. Given the above concerns, I find that the affidavits do not assist the Appellant in establishing that that his sexual orientation is homosexual or bisexual as he has claimed.
Targeting by the Maras
[54] The RPD Panel found that there are "additional reasons to doubt the claimant's allegations about being targeted by the maras."34

[55] The RPD Panel found that the Appellant provided inconsistent testimony regarding his residence history in Honduras and that this testimony impugned the Appellant's credibility. The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the inconsistencies are material and that the RPD focussed unreasonably on a mathematical error.

[56] I do not agree that the RPD Panel erred. The Appellant fears persecution from criminal gangs in Honduras based on his sexual orientation and his refusal to join the gangs. The Appellant's residence history, and his interaction with gangs in Honduras before he left the US, are central to his claim.

[57] The RPD Panel fully canvased the problems with the Appellants testimony with respect to his residency in Honduras in the RPD Reasons.35 I find that it is not necessary to reiterate the RPD's analysis in detail. Based on my own analysis of the record, I find that the Appellant did not provide unprompted, consistent, and coherent testimony to the RPD regarding his residence history in Honduras. I find that the Appellant's residence history in Honduras is central to his claim that he has faced problems with the maras at specific times and in specific locations in Honduras prior to his departure for the US. I agree with the RPD that the inconstancies and contradictions in the Appellant's testimony undermine the Appellant's credibility. I find that the Appellant has not established that he faces a risk of harm from criminal gangs.
Appellant's imputed sexual orientation in Honduras

[58] The Appellant argues he would be persecuted by the gangs in Honduras because he would be perceived to be homosexual or bisexual by the maras. I find that the Appellant does not have a profile in Honduras that would expose him to a serious possibility of persecution from the gangs on the basis of sexual orientation for the reasons that follow.
[59] The Appellant does not provide any details why the gangs in Honduras would perceive him to be bisexual or homosexual.

[60] The RPD Panel asked the Appellant when he revealed to his gay brother that he was attracted to men himself. The Appellant replied that he told his brother that he was attracted to men once the Appellant was in the US.36 The Appellant's mother stated in an affidavit that the Appellant told her he was bisexual when he had already left Honduras and was in the US. There is nothing in the record that anyone in Honduras perceived the Appellant as being gay or bisexual when the Appellant lived in Honduras.

[61] I find that there is insufficient credible evidence in the record to support a finding that the Appellant has a profile in Honduras as a bisexual or homosexual man or that the gangs in Honduras would perceive him as such.
No Section 97 Claim

[62] The RPD found that the Appellant has not established a claim pursuant to section 97 of IRPA.37 The RPD found that there is not sufficient evidence that would provide a foundation, on the balance of probabilities for establishing a personal "risk" for the claimant pursuant to s. 97(1) of the IRPA.

[63] I agree with the RPD. In order for his claim for protection to succeed under section 97(1)(b), an appellant must establish that they face a personal risk that this not shared generally with others in the country of reference.

[64] In this case, the Appellant alleges that he faces a personal risk from gangs because he says that he has been targeted previously by the gangs on the basis of his sexual orientation. The RPD disbelieved that the Appellant had been "threatened or targeted by the maras on the basis of sexual orientation or for any other reason."38 Consequently, the RPD concluded that the Appellant does not face a "personal" risk and dismissed the section 97 claim for this reason.
[65] I agree with the RPD that the Appellant was not threatened or targeted by the maras on the basis of his sexual orientation or for any other reason.

[66] I find that The Appellant has not established through sufficient credible evidence that he faces a personal risk from the gangs in Honduras for reasons because of his sexual orientation or for any other reasons.

[67] The Appellant testified that he owes $XXXX or $XXXX to coyotes (people smugglers) in Guatemala for his passage to the US. The Appellant speculated that the people smugglers in Guatemala to whom he says he owes money might be associated with the gangs in Honduras. The Appellant did not provide any basis for this speculation.

[68] Even it is true that the Appellant owes $XXXX or $XXXX to people smugglers in Guatemala, this does not establish that the Appellant faces a personal risk in Honduras on account of a debt in Guatemala.
CONCLUSION

[69] I find that the Appellant has failed to establish through sufficient credible evidence that he would face a serious possibility of persecution in Honduras or that he would face a likelihood of section 97 harm if he were to return to the Honduras.

[70] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
